---
title: "Performance"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
# Not evaluated: the numbers come from tools/bench.R, which needs live
# servers. Rerun it and update the table when the code it measures changes.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

zugrpc is R on top of zuhttp, so most of a call's time is zuhttp's and the
server's. The design sets four targets for what zugrpc itself adds. This
article reports a measurement for each.

## How it was measured

`tools/bench.R` ran against grpc-go's interop server at v1.67.1 and
`tools/test-server`, both over cleartext HTTP/2 on loopback. The machine
was an Intel Mac running macOS Sequoia 15.7, with R 4.5.2, zugrpc
0.0.0.9000 and zuhttp 0.1.0, on 2026-11-05.

```{r}
# go install google.golang.org/grpc/interop/server@v1.67.1
# server --port 50051 &
# (cd tools && go run ./test-server -grpc_port 50052) &
Rscript tools/bench.R http://127.0.0.1:50051 http://127.0.0.1:50052
```

## Results

| Target | Measured | Met |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A unary call adds under 1 ms to `zu_perform()` | 0.33 ms (median of 2,000 `EmptyCall`s: 0.98 ms against 0.65 ms) | yes |
| Streaming 1 GiB of 16 MiB messages holds at most one message and one chunk | at most 16 MiB live in R | yes |
| 100,000 small messages cost no more each than 10,000 | 19.6 µs each against 23.2 µs | yes |
| `$cancel()` returns within 100 ms of a stalled server | 0.075 ms median, 0.113 ms worst of 20 | yes |

## What the numbers mean

**Unary overhead.** Each `EmptyCall` ran on the same pooled connection,
once through `zu_perform()` and once through `grpc_call()`, alternating.
The difference is zugrpc's work: building the headers, framing the
message, and checking the status and framing of the response. An early
version spent a millisecond more on every call, rebuilding its user-agent
string with `packageVersion()`. It now builds it once per session.

**Large messages.** "Live" is the memory reachable after a full garbage
collection, taken after each message, above what was live before the
call. It never exceeded one 16 MiB message. The stream keeps the pieces
of a message in a list and joins them once, when the message is
complete, so a large message is not copied once per read. The peak heap
over the run was higher, 152 MiB, because R collects garbage lazily: the
joined buffers of earlier messages wait for a collection. Throughput was
1 GiB in 13 s, including the collection forced after each message.

**Small messages.** The cost per message stayed flat from 10,000 to
100,000 messages. A stream that re-joined its whole buffer on each read
would cost more per message as the stream grew. The 64 KiB reads bring
in many small messages at once, and they are split out in one pass.

**Cancel.** `$cancel()` resets the HTTP/2 stream with `RST_STREAM(CANCEL)`
and returns. It does not wait for the server, so a stalled server does not
slow it down. The connection stays pooled for the next call.
